deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Name the 5 trail measurements.
back: Length, width, stride, straddle, group (and gap). Hook: LWSSG.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Track length: from where to where?
back: Tip of the furthest forward toe to the back of the heel pad. Leave out claws and dewclaws.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Track width: how do you measure it?
back: Widest point, at right angles to the length, on the floor of the print.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Step or stride?
back: Step: one print to the next. Stride: same foot to same foot, which is 2 steps. Write down which one you used.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: What is the straddle?
back: The width of the whole trail, outside edge to outside edge, at right angles to travel.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Soft snow print: measure the rim or the floor?
back: The floor. Soft ground pushes the rim out and makes the print look bigger.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: How many prints should you measure?
back: 3 to 5 prints and several strides, then average. Animals change pace.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Do claws count in track length?
back: No. Claws register on and off, so they add error. Note them separately.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Which print is bigger on a deer, front or hind?
back: Front, slightly. Same for dogs and cats. Bears and hares: the hind is longer.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Hare trail: where do the big hind feet land?
back: Ahead of the small front feet. Hind feet are 2 to 4 times as long.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Wolf or dog: the size rule?
back: Front 10 cm (4 in) or more, or hind 9 cm (3.5 in) or more, no claws: likely wolf. 82% of dogs are smaller.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: What is direct register?
back: The hind foot lands in the front print, so only one print shows.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Overstep or understep: which is faster?
back: Overstep (hind lands past the front). Understep is slower.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Walk to trot: what changes in the trail?
back: Stride gets longer and straddle gets narrower.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Bound: what does the pattern show?
back: Hind feet land side by side ahead of the front feet. Hares and squirrels.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Mule deer stot: gap between groups?
back: About 2.4 to 4.6 m (8 to 15 ft). The deer is alarmed.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Mule deer walking stride, North Dakota Game and Fish?
back: About 38 to 64 cm (15 to 25 in). Likely measured print to print.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Moose walking stride, North Dakota Game and Fish?
back: About 71 to 112 cm (28 to 44 in).

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Why do hoof prints splay?
back: Toes spread for grip: downhill, running or in loose soil. Splayed prints look wider.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: Walk, feet together, then stot. What happened?
back: The deer stopped, looked, and fled. Look back along the trail for the cause.

deck: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns
front: A wide straddle suggests what?
back: A heavy bodied animal, or a slow walk.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Name the 5 age bands.
back: Minutes, hours, today, days, a week or more. Give a range, never a minute.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: What is a control print?
back: Your own boot print pressed beside the animal print in the same ground and light. It is the clock you compare against.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: When do you revisit your control print?
back: At 1, 6, 24 and 72 hours. Then you know how that ground ages.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Rain pits inside a print. When was it made?
back: Before the rain.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Clean print on rain spattered ground?
back: Made after the rain.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Frost crystals inside a print?
back: Made before the frost formed, usually last night or earlier.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: A print that cuts through the frost crust?
back: Made after the frost formed, often this morning.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Dark line through silver dewy grass?
back: An animal knocked the dew off after it formed: in the night or this morning.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Snow stopped 4 hours ago and there is snow in the track. Age?
back: At least 4 hours old.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Which ground ages slowest?
back: Mud. A mud print can look fresh for days.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Why do sand prints age fast?
back: The edges dry and slump in sun and wind.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Why can a north slope print fool you?
back: Cold shade keeps edges crisp for days.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Spider web across a print?
back: Hours at least, often a night, since it was made.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Fresh twig break versus old?
back: Fresh: pale, moist, maybe sap. Old: grey and dry.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: What is healing in tracking?
back: Crushed live plants standing back up and repairing. Used to age sign.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Can you age deer scat by colour?
back: Not alone. Diet changes colour. Read moisture, shine and the inside.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Scat that is wet, shiny and smelly with flies?
back: Hours old.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Snow bed with an icy refrozen floor?
back: Older. A dry crisp floor with no refreeze is recent.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Fresh rub clues?
back: Wet bright wood, curled bark on the ground, sap beading.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Sign under 24 hours old and the wind is right. What next?
back: Hunt near it at dawn or dusk.

deck: Aging tracks and sign: hours, days, weeks
front: Why keep a 72 hour weather log?
back: Each print survived some events (rain, frost, wind) and not others. That brackets its age.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Read a dropping in what order?
back: Shape, size, contents, place, age (SSCPA).

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Why gloves and a stick for coyote, fox or wolf scat?
back: They can carry Echinococcus multilocularis, a tapeworm dangerous to people. Rare, but easy to prevent. Wash with soap.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Where was BC's first known Echinococcus multilocularis case?
back: A dog near Quesnel, 2009. Later found in coyotes and foxes there.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Who drops pellets?
back: Deer, elk, moose, hares, rabbits, porcupines.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Rope like scat with tapered ends: which family?
back: Dog family: coyote, wolf, fox, dog.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Segmented scat with blunt ends: which family?
back: Cat family: cougar, bobcat, lynx.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Big pile, never covered, full of berries?
back: Bear. Bears seldom if ever cover scat.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Deer pellet size and shape?
back: About 1.3 cm long, pointed on one end, slightly concave on the other.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Moose pellet size?
back: About 1.9 cm across and 2.5 to 3.8 cm long, rounded both ends, in piles.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Elk pellets versus deer?
back: Bigger and rounder, often dimpled on one end. Check the tracks beside the pile.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Cottontail pellet size?
back: Pea size, about 0.6 cm.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Why are deer droppings soft clumps in summer?
back: Green feed. Woody fall and winter feed makes hard separate pellets.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Wolf or coyote scat by diameter?
back: Wolf: over about 2.5 cm. Coyote: under. Thumb wolf, finger coyote.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Coyote scat usually holds what?
back: Mouse, vole and hare hair, berries, small bones.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Wolf scat usually holds what?
back: Deer, elk or moose hair and bone.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Cougar scat in a scraped pile of needles on a ridge?
back: A cougar marking spot. Deer country, and a kill may be near.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Why do bird droppings have a white cap?
back: Dried urine products. Birds pass urine and feces together.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: A pile of curved grouse droppings under a fir?
back: A night roost.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Grey ball of hair and tiny bones under a perch?
back: An owl pellet, coughed up. Not a dropping.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Deer pellets in a pile beside a flattened oval?
back: The deer bedded or stood here. Scattered pellets mean it was moving.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Can you count deer from pellet piles?
back: No. One deer drops about 13 to 34 pellet groups a day.

deck: Droppings deep dive by species
front: Big piles of curved pellets at a den mouth or under a tree?
back: Porcupine.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Deer bed size?
back: An oval about 0.9 to 1.2 m long; curled deer or fawns smaller.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Elk bed size and pattern?
back: About 1.2 to 1.5 m, many beds together, often near water and wallows.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Moose beds?
back: Bigger, often alone, in willow or timber near water. In late winter they pick shallow snow.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Read a bed: the 4 things?
back: Size, hair, pellets and urine, facing and exit (SHPE).

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Stot groups leaving a bed?
back: The deer was spooked, maybe by you.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Warm bed. What now?
back: Freeze. Glass ahead and to both sides. It left minutes ago and may be watching.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: What mattered most for mule deer day beds in the 2004 study?
back: Site temperature and canopy closure.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Utah mule deer beds: where?
back: Under or near conifers, with less visibility on the north and west sides.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Hunter lore: the classic day bed?
back: Bench in the top third of a slope, near trees, wind behind, view below.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: How does a bedded deer cover itself?
back: Eyes cover below, nose covers behind and above.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Best direction to approach a hillside bed?
back: From the side or above, wind in your face. Not from below on a morning uphill thermal.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Hot day: where do deer bed?
back: Shade: conifers, north slopes, cool draws.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Cold clear day: where do deer bed?
back: Sunny south slopes with cover behind, out of the wind.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Windy day: where do deer bed?
back: Lee side of ridges, low draws, thick timber.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Groups of small beds near an open edge?
back: Does and fawns.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: One big bed alone on an edge with escape cover behind?
back: Maybe a mature buck. Lore, not proof: big does make big beds.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: What marks a bedding area?
back: Many beds, trails between them, pellets of mixed age.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Beginner lean for hunting beds?
back: Ambush the trail between bed and feed at first and last light.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Why not check beds at noon?
back: Deer are in them. You evict them and teach them to move.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Fawn bedded alone in grass?
back: Not abandoned. The doe is close. Leave it.

deck: Beds and bedding areas: finding, reading, using them
front: Old snow bed versus fresh?
back: Old: icy refrozen bowl. Fresh: dry crisp floor.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Why do bucks rub?
back: To mark: antlers and forehead glands leave a visual sign and scent. Glands are most active in autumn.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Do older bucks rub more?
back: Yes. Rubbing tracks testosterone; yearlings make about half as many rubs as prime age bucks.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Rub height that suggests a mature buck?
back: Centred 75 cm or higher (60%). Most rubs are 30 to 105 cm.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Tree size clue?
back: 2.5 to 5 cm often young bucks; over 10 cm usually older. Height is the better clue.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Fresh rub clues?
back: Wet bright wood, curled shavings below, sap. Old: grey and dry.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Which way did the buck come from?
back: The side that is rubbed usually faces where he came from.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: What is a rub line?
back: Rubs in a row facing one way: his route between bed and feed.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: What is a signpost rub?
back: A big tree rubbed year after year, kept up mostly by mature bucks.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Mule deer rubs and scrapes?
back: Fewer rubs, on small conifers and shrubs. Mule deer rarely scrape.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Bark stripped above your head on a big tree?
back: Likely elk.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Willow and alder thrashed and stripped in fall?
back: Bull moose in the rut.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: What is a scrape?
back: A pawed bare oval of soil, soaked with urine, under a licking branch about 1.2 to 1.5 m up.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: What does a buck do to the licking branch?
back: Chews it and rubs it with the preorbital gland near his eye.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: When is most scraping?
back: About 80% from mid October to mid November (northern deer).

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Georgia camera study: buck scrape visits at night?
back: 85%. Doe visits 75%. Only about 5 daylight visits per scrape per season.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Who visited scrapes more, bucks or does?
back: Does, nearly twice as often.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Which scrapes get more daylight visits?
back: Those close to bedding cover (Tip). Field edge scrapes are mostly night.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Wireless trail camera for hunting in BC in October?
back: Unlawful from 1 August to 10 December (Region 1 all year). A memory card camera is not wireless.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Store bought deer urine lure in BC?
back: No. Cervid parts or derivatives from outside BC are banned for hunting; urine can carry CWD.

deck: Rubs and scrapes deep dive
front: Beginner lean for rubs and scrapes?
back: Ambush a fresh rub line near the cover end at first and last light, wind in your face.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Grouse track shape and size?
back: 3 toes forward, 1 short back, about 5 cm. One print ahead of the next.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Duck versus goose track length?
back: Duck about 5 to 7.6 cm, goose about 7.6 to 10 cm. Both webbed.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Game birds walk or hop?
back: Walk: one print ahead of the next. Many songbirds hop in pairs.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Why do grouse tracks look wider in winter?
back: Grouse grow comb like fringes on their toes for snow.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Grouse dust bowl?
back: One round scrape about 20 cm across in dry fine soil, a feather or two.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Quail dust bowls?
back: Many small bowls 7 to 15 cm across: a covey bathed together.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Why do upland birds dust?
back: To help control body parasites.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Pile of white capped curved droppings under a tree?
back: A grouse night roost.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Hole in soft snow with droppings inside and wing marks beside?
back: A grouse snow roost. It dove in and burst out.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: One or two feathers on a trail?
back: Often moult or preening. A pile means something died.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Whole quills pulled clean, in a ring, breastbone left?
back: A bird of prey plucking spot (field rule, 60%).

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Feather shafts cut, blunt, wet or stuck together?
back: A mammal bit them (field rule, 60%).

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Why is the feather rule not proof?
back: Scavengers visit kills and mix the sign.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Tracks end in a fan of wing marks?
back: The bird took off here.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Wing marks and a small hole where vole tracks end?
back: An owl or hawk struck there (Tip).

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Fresh green goose droppings across a field?
back: Geese fed there recently. Geese drop about 6 times an hour while feeding.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: When do you scout a goose field?
back: Late in the afternoon, then set up there next morning (with consent).

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Puff of feathers after your shot?
back: A hit. Mark the fall on a tree or rock and walk straight to it.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Migratory Birds Regulations s. 42: wounded bird?
back: You must ensure it is killed and retrieved as soon as the circumstances permit, and have means to retrieve.

deck: Bird sign: feathers, dusting, droppings, roosts, kill feathers
front: Quail feeding sign?
back: Scratched soil and leaf litter patches under shrubs near cover.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Fresh signs of recent bear activity?
back: Tracks, scat, overturned logs, dug up anthills.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Ravens, magpies, crows or jays gathered in one spot?
back: Maybe a carcass or gut pile that has drawn a bear. Be careful.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Covered carcass in cover?
back: A cache. The owner (cougar or bear) is close and coming back. Leave.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Cougar kill style?
back: Little chase, bites to neck and head, dragged to cover, covered neatly, organs eaten first, tidy.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: How long does a cougar stay near a kill?
back: It feeds for about 6 to 8 days.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Wolf kill style?
back: Chase, bites to rear, flanks and throat, fed at the kill, rumen open, big bones cracked, remains spread.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Coyote kill style?
back: Throat bites, smaller bones broken, small prey, fed at the kill.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Bear cache?
back: Dirt and debris raked over the carcass; ground looks rototilled. Bears defend caches.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Long claw scrape marks over 61 cm on a kill?
back: Cougar. Bobcat marks are 41 cm or less.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Signs a struggle happened here?
back: Trampled plants, broken branches, blood sprayed on ground or brush.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Bites with no bruising under the hide?
back: Made after death: scavenging, not the kill.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Found a carcass: the 5 steps?
back: Stop, look and listen, read from afar, back out loud, tell and report (SLRBT).

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: BC number for wildlife danger to people?
back: RAPP (Report All Poachers and Polluters): 1 877 952 7277, 24 hours.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: When are bear surprises most likely?
back: Loud water, wind or rain, dawn, dusk, night, thick cover and bends.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Why are hunters at higher risk of bear encounters?
back: Quiet, using calls and scents, often alone, handling carcasses.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Leaving your carcass to return later?
back: Move it at least 200 m from the gut pile. Bears go to the gut pile first.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Hang meat in bear country: numbers?
back: At least 3.5 m up, 1.5 m from trees, in plain view, 100 m from camp.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Coming back to your kill?
back: Approach from upwind, glass first, make lots of noise.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Your carcass has been moved or buried?
back: Do not approach. Leave immediately and report.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Why not drag the carcass back to camp?
back: It lays a scent trail a bear can follow to where you sleep.

deck: Predator sign and kill sites: reading them and staying safe
front: Who does what while field dressing in bear country?
back: One works, one watches with spray and rifle. Make noise.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Hit site search: the 5 steps?
back: Landmark from your spot, flag where you shot, walk in from the side, search a 3 m circle, check the bullet path beyond.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: What do you look for in the 3 m circle?
back: Hair, blood, bone, tissue, scuffs (HBBTS).

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Pink froth and spongy pink tissue?
back: Lung hit (70%).

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Green or brown matter and a sour smell?
back: Gut hit. Back out 6 to 8 hours or more.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Bone chips with marrow and little blood?
back: Possibly a leg or shoulder hit.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: White fat with a green smear?
back: Paunch (gut) hit.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Dark red blood, no bubbles?
back: Liver. Back out 4 to 6 hours (hunter education).

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: What happens to blood colour as it dries?
back: It darkens and dulls, then looks brown. Rain lightens it.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Which way does a blood drop tail point?
back: The way the animal was moving.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Round drops with no tails?
back: The animal was standing or moving slowly (Tip).

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Blood high on brush on both sides of the trail?
back: A pass through, bleeding well.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Blood low and on one side only?
back: Maybe no exit hole. Expect less blood.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: A fine mist of tiny drops at nose height?
back: Blood breathed out: often a lung sign (Tip).

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Deer blood volume and lethal loss?
back: About 7% of body weight (about 4 L for 60 kg). Losing about a third may cause shock or death.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: How to calibrate your eye for blood amount?
back: Pour a cup (250 mL) of coloured water on leaves and look at it.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Most common reason a blood trail stops?
back: Clotting. Also fat or hair plugs, no exit hole, or a gut or muscle hit.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: No blood in the first 10 m. A miss?
back: Not necessarily. Search hair, tissue and tracks; wait and look again.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Where do wounded deer usually go?
back: Downhill, into thick cover, toward water, often on a game trail.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Heart or lung rifle hit: how far does a deer usually go?
back: Usually dead within about 137 m (150 yd).

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Tracking a wounded animal in bear country?
back: Bears come to wounded animals. One tracks, one watches. Talk.

deck: Blood, hair and tissue: reading the hit and the terrain of recovery
front: Can you follow a blood trail with your rifle after legal hours?
back: No. Following a trail with a firearm is hunting; no hunting after hours or with a light.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Before you follow a track, 3 questions?
back: Fresh (hours, not days)? An animal you can legally hunt? Legal light left?

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Common tracking mistake about which trail to follow?
back: Following the first tracks you see, often a doe and fawns wandering.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Where do your eyes go while tracking?
back: Glance down at the next print, then look 40 to 100 m ahead.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: The 3 and 10 rule?
back: 3 seconds on the track, 10 seconds on the cover ahead (Tip).

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: How do you see faint tracks?
back: Get low and look toward a low side light. Shadows show the print.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Why is midday hard for tracking?
back: Overhead sun flattens tracks; no shadows.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: What is a track stick?
back: A stick or ski pole with 2 bands set at step and stride. Sweep it from the last track to find the next.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Why reset the track stick bands?
back: Stride changes with terrain and fatigue.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Lost the trail. First move?
back: Back to the last clear print, flag it, circle about 10 m, then 20 m.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Why not walk on ahead when you lose a trail?
back: You stamp out the next print and add a second set of tracks.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Trail shows feeding and wandering?
back: It is close. Slow right down and glass every direction.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Trail shows a straight trot?
back: It is travelling. You can move faster.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Crunchy snow tracking trick?
back: Walk like a deer: a few quick steps, then stop (Hal Blood).

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Trail turns downwind?
back: Leave it and loop around so your scent does not reach the deer.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Trail starts to hook back?
back: It may be bedding or watching its back trail. Stop, glass, swing wide.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Why can a 2 day old buck track still pay off?
back: White tailed bucks often stay in about 26 to 31 km² (Benoit lore).

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Tracking as a pair: jobs?
back: Tracker reads the trail; spotter watches ahead and to the sides. Swap often.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: When do you stop following?
back: No legal light for a recovery, bad weather, land you may not hunt, or not enough time and energy to get back.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: Before you start following, navigation?
back: Pin the truck, record a GPS track, set a turnaround time, tell someone.

deck: Following a track to the animal: technique and patience
front: FLAW checks before a follow?
back: Fresh, Light, Ahead, Wind.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Wet snow or powder: which shows detail?
back: Wet snow captures a print well; powder leaves holes with little detail.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Crust snow tracking?
back: Few prints, just scratches, and loud walking. Slow down or wait for softer snow.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Best tracking snow?
back: A light fresh snow on firm ground.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Why do snow prints grow?
back: Sun melts them out bigger and rounder over days. Measure fresh prints only.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Melted out fawn print risk?
back: It can look like an elk print. Use shape, toes and pattern, not size.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Snow depth deer struggle in?
back: Past about 30 cm; they leave slopes past about 50 cm. Moose fine to about 40 cm.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: What does mud show best?
back: Toes, pad shape and nails.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Mud trap?
back: Mud ages slowest. A crisp print can be days old.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Fresh mud print clues?
back: Water seeping into the floor, shiny wet walls, a pushed up rim.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Wet sand versus dry sand?
back: Wet sand holds clear shapes. Dry sand slumps into bowls; read spacing instead.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Why do sand prints age fast?
back: The edges dry out quickly in sun and wind.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Dust as a tracking ground?
back: Fine detail, but rare and erased by wind. A fresh dust print has a thin raised rim.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Deer print on top of a tire tread?
back: Made after the vehicle passed. On top came last.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: No prints in leaves and duff: what to read?
back: Flipped leaves, scuffed moss, pressed duff, moved stones.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Which way did it go through grass?
back: Bent stems lie the way the animal moved.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Natural track traps?
back: Creek crossings, road edges, fence lines, field edges: where tracks pile up.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Homemade track trap?
back: Smooth a strip of dirt on a trail in the evening; check it in the morning.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: When does avalanche terrain start?
back: Around 30 degrees once there is enough snow to slide.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: November river or lake ice?
back: Not trustworthy. Do not cross to save a kilometre.

deck: Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust
front: Why do tracks of one animal look so different?
back: Ground (snow, mud, dust, sand) and speed change how a track looks.
